title: Would you actually eat a 'bake-it-yourself' protein mug cake? Looking for honest opinions (not selling anything)
body:
Hey all, a couple of us are exploring an idea and want brutal feedback before we build anything.

Idea: a single-serve ~50g sachet (around 10g protein, eggless, trying for gluten-free). Add water or milk in a mug, then microwave about 1 min or air fryer about 10 min (OTG or pressure cooker also work). You get a warm brownie or cake.

Things we really want to hear about:
1. Have you made whey mug cakes at home? What went wrong? Dry, rubbery, the whey aftertaste?
2. Is 10g protein per serving worth it, or would you rather just have a shake plus a normal dessert?
3. What would you pay for one sachet before it feels like a ripoff?
4. Flavours: chocolate, or something Indian like gulab jamun, kesar-pista, filter coffee?
5. Do protein-snack labels in India feel trustworthy to you right now?

There's a 2-minute anonymous survey if you'd rather answer there: [SURVEY LINK]

No brand, no link to buy, no DMs. Happy to share what we learn back here. Mods, please remove if this isn't allowed.

title: Eggless microwave/air-fryer mug cakes: what makes them good or terrible for you?
body:
Quick question for people who bake small desserts at home. Microwave mug cakes, air fryer brownies, pressure-cooker cakes, all of it.

We're researching a ready-mix mug cake idea: an eggless single-serve sachet, just add milk or water, with some extra protein from milk or pea protein. Before going further, we'd love to know:

- How often do you get a sweet craving that you'd fix with a quick homemade dessert instead of ordering in?
- What usually goes wrong with mug cakes for you? Texture, sweetness, uneven cooking?
- Which appliance do you actually use: microwave, air fryer, OTG, or cooker?
- Would Indian flavours (elaichi, kesar-pista, gajar halwa, chai-spice) interest you more than chocolate or vanilla?
- Does 'protein' on a dessert make you more or less interested?

If you'd like to answer anonymously, there's a short survey: [SURVEY LINK]

Not selling anything. Recipes and tips are very welcome too!

title: Validating a small idea: single-serve protein mug cakes for Indian kitchens
body:
India's protein moment is real. Instamart reports protein-related orders up about 150% in two years, and around 86% of surveyed snackers say protein matters to them. But consumers are also tired of chalky bars, 'protein washing' and premium prices. Only about a third say they'd pay extra.

We're testing a simple idea before building it: an eggless single-serve sachet (about 50g, about 10g protein). Mix it with milk or water and bake it in about a minute in the microwave or about 10 minutes in an air fryer. It's meant as a dessert swap, not a supplement.

I'd value candid input, especially from food/FMCG, D2C, nutrition and quick-commerce folks:
• Is this a real habit, or a novelty purchase you'd make once?
• What price per sachet makes sense next to a ₹40 chocolate bar or a ₹100 protein bar?
• Where would it sell best: Q-comm, D2C, gyms, or corporate pantries?

A 2-minute survey for anyone who'd be a potential user: [SURVEY LINK]
Comments and DMs with tough questions are very welcome.

#FoodInnovation #ConsumerResearch #D2CIndia #Protein
